title: How Embalming Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and modern practice of embalming, from ancient Egyptian, Chinchorro, Guanche, and Canary Islands methods through Charlemagne, Renaissance injection experiments by da Vinci, and 19th-century chemical embalming popularized by Dr. Thomas Holmes during the Civil War. They walk through the modern arterial and cavity embalming process, the chemicals involved (formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde), cosmetic restoration of the face, debate over whether people should view the body, and environmental concerns about embalming fluid in cemeteries and cremation. The episode closes with a listener email correcting the pronunciation of Waukesha, Wisconsin.

segments.title: Opening banter and Lincoln's embalming
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Famed and Legendary Deaths suite, discuss finding the topic on HowStuffWorks, and recall Abraham Lincoln's 19-day journey to Springfield enabled by Thomas Holmes's chemical embalming. They mention the Merchant's House Museum and early embalming history of masking decay with lilies and ice.

segments.title: Ancient embalming origins
segments.summary: The hosts trace embalming to ancient times, citing possible early cases in Spain's Lavella, and describe Egyptian methods including organ removal, natron, resins, and tiered processes by social class. They note Herodotus's account and the difference between preserved mummies and skeletonization.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a short break before resuming the history.

segments.title: Global embalming traditions and Renaissance advances
segments.summary: The hosts cover the Chinchorro of Chile, the Guanche of the Canary Islands, Hivaro head preservation, Buddhist monk mummies, and cultures that avoided embalming. They then discuss Charlemagne's tomb, the medieval decline, and da Vinci's injection method during the Renaissance.

segments.title: 19th-century chemical embalming and the Civil War
segments.summary: French and Italian researchers advanced chemical embalming for medical students, and Thomas Holmes brought it to the US, including on Civil War battlefields where the Union Army hired embalming surgeons. The hosts discuss early chemicals like arsenic and mercury chloride and the environmental danger of arsenic leaching into soil.

segments.title: Funeral industry roles
segments.summary: The hosts discuss modern job titles in the funeral industry, including funeral directors, embalmers, trade embalmers, and restorative artists, and the emotional demands of the work. They mention the TV show Six Feet Under.

segments.title: Cosmetic preparation: face, eyes, and mouth
segments.summary: The hosts describe shaving, closing eyes with skin glue or eye caps, wiring or sewing the mouth shut, and using cotton to fill out the face. They discuss personal appearance choices and an anecdote about Marlon Brando.

segments.title: Arterial embalming process and fluids
segments.summary: Drawing on a Guardian interview, the hosts explain the arterial process: incision near the collarbone, cannulating the carotid artery and jugular vein, pumping fluid while draining blood, massaging limbs, and cavity treatment with a trocar. They explain formaldehyde and glutaraldehyde's roles in preservation and disinfection and the typical fluid volume.
